title: UK Picks Tekever AR5 in £400M Watchkeeper Replacement as L3Harris Lands $4.7B PAC-3 Propulsion Award
subhead: Britain's new defence secretary Wes Streeting confirmed the Portuguese firm's AR5 drone to replace the Army's ageing Watchkeeper fleet, while L3Harris won a $4.7 billion Lockheed contract to expand Patriot interceptor production — both moves point to a European and US push to rebuild drone and missile industrial capacity.

sections.heading: UK Confirms Tekever AR5 to Replace Watchkeeper in £400M Deal
sections.body:
The UK Ministry of Defence has confirmed that Portugal's Tekever will supply its twin-engine AR5 surveillance drone to replace the British Army's ageing Thales Watchkeeper fleet, in a contract worth up to £400 million ($532 million) over ten years, according to Aviation Week and UK press reports. The initial order covers six AR5 air systems, with up to 24 delivered by 2029. The drones will be built at Tekever's new Swindon factory, sustaining jobs at its sites in Bristol, Southampton and Aberporth in Wales.

New defence secretary Wes Streeting framed the deal as both a capability and industrial decision: 'Proven in Ukraine and designed to protect British soldiers globally, we've chosen the UK-based Tekever AR5 drone to supply our personnel with kit that will keep them ahead of emerging threats.' The AR5, which can carry up to 50kg of sensors and has already been used by Ukrainian forces, is being delivered under the programme name Corvus, with entry into service expected later this year.
sections.whyItMatters: The choice of a Portuguese firm over a UK incumbent (Thales) signals that London is prioritising proven, battle-tested drone capability and speed over domestic incumbency — and the Swindon factory anchors a sovereign production line that can scale.

sections.heading: L3Harris Wins $4.7B PAC-3 Propulsion Award as Patriot Production Ramps
sections.body:
L3Harris Technologies said on Tuesday it received an undefinitized contract award from Lockheed Martin valued at $4.7 billion over seven years to produce propulsion systems for the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) interceptor, per RTTNews and MSN. The award is tied to expanding production at L3Harris' Arkansas plants, with new facilities expected to boost missile output by 2027, according to Interesting Engineering.

The contract comes as the US Army has requested over 2,700 PAC-3 MSE interceptors in its next fiscal budget — a sharp jump from the 357 previously funded — after the US military fired nearly 1,500 Patriot interceptors in the Iran war, per The Diplomat and ABC News. Lockheed produced a record 500+ interceptors in 2024, but wartime consumption has outpaced that rate.
sections.whyItMatters: The award is a direct industrial response to the Iran war's interceptor burn rate: the US is effectively re-tooling its missile supply chain to rebuild a stockpile that wartime demand has drawn down faster than production can replace.

sections.heading: US Arms Bottleneck Leaves Taiwan and Japan Queuing Behind Ukraine and Iran
sections.body:
US Congress has approved $500 million for Taiwan defense even as the Trump administration continues to hesitate on the larger $14 billion package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors and NASAMS air defense systems, per today's headlines and Defense News. The Diplomat reports that Taiwan has received at least four conflicting explanations for the delay since May, with officials variously citing the Iran war ('Epic Fury'), a policy review, and Trump's own framing of the sales as 'a very good negotiating chip' with China.

The bottleneck is structural: the US has also told Japan that delivery of 400 Tomahawk cruise missiles will be delayed two years to meet Iran-war drawdown demands. Taiwan's order of 102 interceptors and Japan's sit in the same production queue as Ukraine and Iran resupply. The US Army's request for 2,700+ interceptors 'merely scratches' the surface of the demand, The Diplomat notes.
sections.whyItMatters: The Taiwan and Japan delays expose a core tension of the Iran war: finite US missile stocks are being prioritised for one theatre, forcing Washington to ration deliveries to its most exposed Asian allies at the very moment it is trying to deter China.

sections.heading: US Navy Nears F/A-XX Decision Between Boeing and Northrop Grumman
sections.body:
The Pentagon has decided which company will build the US Navy's next-generation stealth fighter and could announce the winner in the coming weeks, two people briefed on the matter told AOL/Reuters. Boeing and Northrop Grumman are competing for the F/A-XX contract to replace the ageing F/A-18 Super Hornet, a program worth hundreds of billions over its lifetime, per Forbes. The Navy has yet to formally announce the award.

The decision follows a period of uncertainty: Bloomberg reported in May that Pentagon leadership had shifted to supporting the program after previously pushing back on it. The F/A-XX is a central pillar of the Navy's plan to confront China in the Pacific.
sections.whyItMatters: A Boeing win would be a major lifeline for the company's fighter business after years of commercial and defense turbulence; a Northrop win would cement its rise as a prime airframe house. Either way, the award locks in the Navy's carrier-airpower roadmap for decades.

sections.heading: GE Aerospace to Buy Castings Supplier for $11.75B to Fix Engine Bottleneck
sections.body:
GE Aerospace said on Tuesday it would acquire castings supplier Consolidated Precision Products for $11.75 billion, bringing a key part of its engine supply chain in-house as it races to expand production capacity, per Reuters. The deal targets a persistent bottleneck in engine castings that has constrained output of military and commercial engines alike.

The acquisition is part of a broader industry push to secure critical components as defense and commercial demand collide. GE Aerospace supplies engines for platforms including the F-35 and various military aircraft, and the castings shortage has been a recurring constraint on delivery timelines.
sections.whyItMatters: Vertical integration of a critical casting supplier reflects how defense primes are responding to a demand surge that has exposed fragile, single-source supply chains — a pattern now visible across engines, interceptors and drones.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Fire Point Scales Cruise Missile Production as US-Iran Pause Holds
sections.body:
Ukrainian startup Fire Point is mass-producing cruise missiles that are striking deep into Russia, per today's headlines, building on its Flamingo cruise missile line. The company, which also makes the FP-1 long-range strike drone, is accelerating plans for a European missile defense system after an agreement with German radar maker Hensoldt, with first interceptors hoped for by year-end, Reuters reported in June.

Separately, the US-Iran war entered a pause for a third consecutive night as diplomatic efforts intensify, with oil prices sliding below $90 on de-escalation hopes. But the conflict is not static: Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen launched strikes on several Saudi cities on Tuesday, and Iran has threatened new missiles and a Gulf exclusion zone, per Reuters. Iran also warned Ukraine of retaliation after a deadly Caspian Sea strike on a vessel.
sections.whyItMatters: Fire Point's shift from strike drones to cruise missiles and now ballistic-missile defense shows Ukraine's defense industry maturing into a full-spectrum producer. The US-Iran pause, meanwhile, is fragile — Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia show the war's periphery remains active even as the core front cools.

bottomLine: Today's defense industry news is dominated by industrial capacity: the UK's £400M Tekever AR5 deal and L3Harris' $4.7B PAC-3 propulsion award both reflect a global scramble to rebuild drone and missile production lines that wartime demand has exposed as too thin. The US arms bottleneck laid out by The Diplomat — Taiwan and Japan queuing behind Ukraine and Iran for finite Patriot and Tomahawk stocks — is the strategic crux, forcing Washington to ration deliveries to Asian allies while fighting in the Middle East. The imminent F/A-XX decision and GE Aerospace's $11.75B castings acquisition round out a picture of an industry re-tooling at every level, from airframes to engine castings to interceptors.
sources: Aviation Week, AOL/Business Live, MSN, RTTNews, Interesting Engineering, The Diplomat, Defense News, Forbes, AOL/Reuters, Bloomberg, Reuters, ABC News, CBS News
